condition: (no condition) minimum daily minimum temperature in the period

sections.definition: The lowest daily minimum temperature during Summer (Jun–Aug). Flowering, berry growth and veraison (Dec–Feb in the Southern Hemisphere).
sections.why: Night-time temperature. It drives frost and cold damage and how well acidity and color are kept. Splitting it by growth stage shows which part of the season the change is concentrated in.
sections.guide: - A positive slope means the value is rising. Compare with other months and seasons of the same variable to find when the change happens.
sections.caveats:
- Cold-air pooling on valley floors is poorly captured by a ~50 km grid.
- A systematically generated statistic, so its link to grower decisions is less direct than the core indicators.
sections.references:
- Computed from the team data workbook, D_ daily sheets (scripts/generate_families.py)

sections.guide: - A positive slope means the value is rising. Compare with other months and seasons of the same variable to find when the change happens.
sections.caveats:
- Daily mean wind at 2 m, so gusts are not captured.

name: Jan (deep dormancy) warmer-than-normal days
short: Number of days with a maximum temperature above the normal (same period, 2001–2010) top 10% during Jan (deep dormancy)
condition: above the normal (2001–2010) 90th percentile

sections.definition: The number of days with a maximum temperature above the normal (same period, 2001–2010) top 10% during Jan (deep dormancy). Jan in the Northern Hemisphere (Jul in the Southern), the vine's deep dormancy stage. The baseline is the region's own 2001–2010 values for the same period, so each region is compared with its own normal.
sections.why: Even a small shift in the average can sharply change how often extreme days occur. This compares how much more often 'unusual days' happen in each region on the same scale.
sections.guide: - By definition, 2001–2010 averages about 10% of the days in the period (5% of rainy days for heavy rain). A rise after that means such days are becoming more frequent.
sections.caveats:
- The baseline period (2001–2010) may itself already be warmer than older norms.
- A systematically generated indicator.
sections.references:
- ETCCDI percentile-index method applied per period (scripts/generate_families.py)
- NASA POWER — https://power.larc.nasa.gov/

sections.definition: The number of days with a minimum temperature below the normal bottom 10% during Season year (Oct–Sep). The season year from the month after harvest to the next harvest (Apr–Mar in the Southern Hemisphere). The baseline is the region's own 2001–2010 values for the same period, so each region is compared with its own normal.
sections.why: Even a small shift in the average can sharply change how often extreme days occur. This compares how much more often 'unusual days' happen in each region on the same scale.
sections.guide: - By definition, 2001–2010 averages about 10% of the days in the period (5% of rainy days for heavy rain). A rise after that means such days are becoming more frequent.
sections.caveats:
- The baseline period (2001–2010) may itself already be warmer than older norms.
- A systematically generated indicator.
sections.references:
- ETCCDI percentile-index method applied per period (scripts/generate_families.py)
- NASA POWER — https://power.larc.nasa.gov/

sections.definition: R99p is a standard index defined by the WMO Expert Team on Climate Change Detection and Indices (ETCCDI): total precipitation on days above the normal top 1% of rainy days, computed per season year (Oct–Sep; Southern Hemisphere Apr–Mar).
sections.why: Climate research worldwide uses these same definitions, so your region's change can be compared directly with results for other regions in papers and reports. It also lets you say in a presentation that standard indices reach the same conclusion.
sections.guide: - Slope direction and units follow the index definition. Percentile indices use 2001–2010 as the baseline.
sections.caveats:
- The official ETCCDI uses calendar years, a 1961–1990 baseline and 5-day calendar windows for percentiles; here it is simplified to season years, a 2001–2010 baseline and whole-period percentiles.
- ~50 km grid values.
sections.references:
- Zhang, X. et al. (2011), Indices for monitoring changes in extremes based on daily temperature and precipitation data — https://doi.org/10.1002/wcc.147
- NASA POWER — https://power.larc.nasa.gov/
